summary.text: Dark energy is a proposed form of energy that affects the universe on its largest scales and drives its accelerating expansion.
In the lambda-CDM model it makes up about 68% of the mass-energy of today's observable universe, though its density is very low.
Its first evidence came from supernova measurements showing the expansion is speeding up, and its exact nature remains a mystery.

facts.label: Why it dominates
facts.value: It is uniform across space, despite its low density

facts.label: Einstein's symbol
facts.value: The cosmological constant, written as capital lambda

items.prompt: Before the supernova results, scientists expected the pull of matter to slow the universe's expansion over time. What did the measurements show?

options.label: The expansion is steady
The expansion has stopped
The expansion is accelerating
The universe is contracting

items.explain: Comparing supernova distances with redshift showed that the universe's expansion is accelerating.

items.prompt: Why can Type Ia supernovae be used to measure distances well?

options.label: They have a constant luminosity
They are always the closest explosions
They happen at regular intervals in time
They are all found in the same galaxy

items.explain: Type Ia supernovae have constant luminosity, which means they can be used to accurately measure distances.

items.prompt: Dark energy's density is far lower than the matter inside galaxies, yet it makes up most of the universe's mass-energy. What explains this?

options.label: It grows denser with time and distance
It is concentrated into a few large clumps
It is spread uniformly across all of space
It was measured with the wrong instrument

items.explain: Its density is very low, but it dominates the mass-energy content because it is uniform across space.

items.prompt: If dark energy is a property of space itself, what happens as the universe expands and more space comes into existence?

options.label: The energy is thinned out and weakens
The energy stays fixed, so the expansion slows
The energy turns into ordinary matter
More of it appears, causing accelerated expansion

items.explain: This energy is a property of space, so it is not diluted as space expands; more space brings more of it, causing accelerated expansion.

items.prompt: Einstein added a constant to hold the universe still, so it neither grew nor shrank. What was wrong with that static picture?

options.label: Hubble showed it needed a second constant
The constant was too large to measure
It made the universe expand much too quickly
The balance is unstable, so small changes would run away

items.explain: The static balance is unstable: slight expansion releases vacuum energy and leads to more expansion, and slight contraction continues.

items.prompt: How do the two main candidates, a cosmological constant and scalar fields, differ?

options.label: The constant is the more dynamic of the two
The constant stays the same, while scalar fields can vary
Scalar fields never change in time or space
Neither one can affect expansion

items.explain: A cosmological constant would remain constant across time and space, while scalar fields can vary.

paragraphs.heading: A push on the largest scales
paragraphs.text: Dark energy is a proposed kind of energy that acts on the universe as a whole, at the very biggest scales. Its main effect is to make the expansion of the universe speed up. It also slows down the rate at which structures form. Nobody yet knows what it actually is, and scientists have put forward many possible explanations.

paragraphs.heading: Thin but everywhere
paragraphs.text: If the standard lambda-CDM model of cosmology is right, dark energy makes up about 68% of all the mass and energy in today's observable universe. Dark matter supplies 27%, ordinary matter 5%, and things like neutrinos and photons hardly count. Yet dark energy is spread very thin: about 7×10⁻³⁰ g/cm³, far less dense than the matter inside galaxies. It still wins overall because it is spread evenly through all of space.

paragraphs.heading: Clues from supernovae
paragraphs.text: The first evidence came from measuring a kind of supernova called Type Ia. These always shine with the same true brightness, so how bright one looks tells you how far away it is. Its redshift tells you how fast it is moving away. Comparing the distance with the speed showed that the expansion is getting faster. Before this, scientists expected the pull of gravity from everything in the universe to slow the expansion down over time.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein's constant
paragraphs.text: The simplest candidate is the cosmological constant, a fixed extra term that can be added to Einstein's equations of general relativity. It amounts to giving empty space its own energy, often called vacuum energy. Because that energy belongs to space itself, it does not thin out as space grows. As more space appears, more of this energy appears with it, and the expansion speeds up. The other main idea is a scalar field, such as quintessence, whose energy can change across time and space.

paragraphs.heading: The greatest blunder
paragraphs.text: Einstein first brought in the constant, which he wrote as Λ (capital lambda), to make his equations describe a universe that stays still, with the constant balancing gravity. That balance turned out to be unstable: a small expansion would feed more expansion, and a small contraction would keep contracting. Then Edwin Hubble's observations in 1929 showed that the universe seems to be expanding, not static. Einstein reportedly called his failure to predict a changing universe his greatest blunder.

paragraphs.heading: How the case was made
paragraphs.text: Direct evidence arrived in 1998, when two teams, led by Riess and by Perlmutter, used supernovae to show the expansion is speeding up, and the Lambda-CDM model took the lead. In 2000, the BOOMERanG and Maxima experiments studied the cosmic microwave background and found the total density of the universe is close to 100% of the critical density. In 2001, the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey found that matter supplies only around 30% of it. The large gap between those two numbers points to a smooth spread of dark energy making up the rest.
